title: Version Control: Commits, Branching, and Merging

blocks.text: Imagine working on a team project where everyone edits the same document simultaneously. How do you keep track of changes, avoid overwriting each other's work, and ensure that the final product is cohesive? This is where version control systems come into play.

blocks.markdown: Version control systems (VCS) are essential tools in software engineering, enabling teams to manage changes to source code over time. They allow multiple developers to work on a project simultaneously without conflict, maintain a history of changes, and facilitate the merging of different code branches.

blocks.title: Version Control System (VCS)
blocks.text: A Version Control System is a tool that helps manage changes to source code over time, allowing multiple developers to collaborate on a project.

blocks.markdown: One of the key features of a VCS is branching. Branching allows developers to diverge from the main line of development and continue to work independently without affecting the main codebase. This is particularly useful in a team setting where different members may be working on different features or bug fixes simultaneously.

blocks.title: Branching Workflow
blocks.text: A branching workflow involves creating branches for new features, bug fixes, or experiments. These branches can be merged back into the main branch once the work is complete and tested.

blocks.title: Creating and Merging a Branch
blocks.prompt: Suppose you are working on a new feature for a project. Describe the steps you would take to create a branch, work on the feature, and merge it back into the main branch.

steps.text: 1. **Create a new branch**: Use the command `git branch feature-xyz` to create a new branch named `feature-xyz`.
2. **Switch to the new branch**: Use `git checkout feature-xyz` to switch to the new branch.
3. **Develop the feature**: Make changes and commit them using `git commit -m 'Add new feature xyz'`.
4. **Merge the branch**: Switch back to the main branch using `git checkout main` and merge the feature branch using `git merge feature-xyz`.
5. **Resolve any conflicts**: If there are conflicts, resolve them manually and commit the changes.

blocks.answer: The steps involve creating a branch, switching to it, developing the feature, merging it back into the main branch, and resolving any conflicts.

blocks.markdown: Merge conflicts occur when changes in different branches affect the same part of a file and cannot be automatically reconciled by the VCS. Resolving these conflicts requires manual intervention to decide which changes to keep.

blocks.title: Merge Conflicts
blocks.text: Merge conflicts can arise when two branches modify the same line in a file. They must be resolved manually to ensure the codebase remains functional.

blocks.title: Resolving a Merge Conflict
blocks.prompt: You attempt to merge a feature branch into the main branch and encounter a merge conflict. How do you resolve it?

steps.text: 1. **Identify the conflict**: Use `git status` to see which files have conflicts.
2. **Open the conflicting file**: Open the file in a text editor to see the conflicting changes.
3. **Resolve the conflict**: Edit the file to manually resolve the conflicts, choosing which changes to keep.
4. **Mark as resolved**: Use `git add <file>` to mark the conflict as resolved.
5. **Commit the resolution**: Commit the resolved changes using `git commit`.

blocks.answer: Resolving a merge conflict involves identifying the conflict, manually editing the file to resolve it, marking it as resolved, and committing the changes.

blocks.markdown: A well-structured commit history is crucial for debugging and understanding the evolution of a codebase. Each commit should represent a logical unit of work, with a clear and descriptive message.

blocks.title: Commit Message Best Practices
blocks.text: A good commit message should be concise yet descriptive. For example, `git commit -m 'Fix bug in user authentication flow'` clearly indicates what was changed and why.

points: Version control systems enable collaborative development by managing changes to code.
Branching allows for parallel development, while merge conflicts require manual resolution.
A clear commit history aids in debugging and understanding code changes.
